questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Monochromatic light is incident normally on a single slit. The resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen. The width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern is x.

The distance between the single slit and the screen is much greater than the slit width and is unchanged.

The light source is replaced by another light source of light with twice the wavelength, and the single slit is replaced by one that has half the slit width.

What is the linear width of the new central maximum in terms of x?
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light is incident normally on a single slit. The resulting diffraction pattern is observed on a screen. The width of the central maximum of the diffraction pattern is x. The distance between the single slit and the screen is much greater than the slit width and is unchanged. The light source is replaced by another light source of light with twice the wavelength, and the single slit is replaced by one that has half the slit width. What is the linear width of the new central maximum in terms of x? A 0.5x B x C 2x D 4x

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Small-angle single-slit relation with two simultaneous factor changes.
questions.misconception: Thinking the two changes cancel

explanation.body:
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$. Since the slit-screen distance $D$ is much greater than the slit width, the angle is small.

$\theta = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}x}{D} = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so $x = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{b}$.

New width: $x' = \dfrac{2(2\lambda)D}{b/2} = \dfrac{8\lambda D}{b} = 4x$.

perOption.A: Wrong proportionality; $x \propto \lambda/b$, so both changes widen the pattern.
perOption.B: Assumes the two changes cancel, but doubling λ and halving b both increase the width.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two changes.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. First and second order images are observed at angles of diffraction $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ respectively. [Diagram: monochromatic light incident normally on a vertical grating; diffracted beams to a screen labelled n = 0, n = 1 and n = 2 on each side, with $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ measured from the central n = 0 direction.] What is the relation between the angles of diffraction and between the intensities of light in the two orders? (angles of diffraction; intensities) A $\theta_2 = 2\theta_1$; same B $\theta_2 = 2\theta_1$; second order dimmer C $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$; same D $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$; second order dimmer

stemImage.alt: Question 15: Monochromatic light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. First and second order images are observed at angles of diffraction 1 and 2 respectively. d

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that sin θ, not θ, scales with order, and recalling that higher orders are dimmer.
questions.misconception: Assuming $\theta \propto n$ rather than $\sin\theta \propto n$

explanation.body:
$\sin\theta_1 = \dfrac{(1)\lambda}{d}$ and $\sin\theta_2 = \dfrac{(2)\lambda}{d}$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$.

The rate of increase of $\sin\theta$ decreases as $\theta$ increases from 0 to 90°, so $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$.

At higher orders, since the distance travelled by the light increases, intensity decreases, so the second order is dimmer.

perOption.A: Assumes $\theta \propto n$, but it is $\sin\theta$ that is proportional to $n$; also intensity is not the same.
perOption.B: Assumes $\theta \propto n$; it is $\sin\theta$ that doubles.
perOption.C: Angle relation is right, but higher orders are dimmer.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The lens of a spy satellite orbiting at 200 km has a diameter of 35 cm. What is the shortest distance this camera can resolve on the surface of the Earth if a wavelength of 500 nm is used? A $2.9\times10^{-4}$ m B 0.14 m C 0.29 m D 2.9 m

stemImage.alt: Question 16: The lens of a spy satellite orbiting at 200 km has a diameter of 35 cm. What is the shortest distance this camera can resolve on the surface of the Earth if a w

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Rayleigh criterion plus small-angle geometry with unit conversions.
questions.misconception: Unit/power-of-ten errors with km and nm

explanation.body:
Using the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b} = \dfrac{x}{D}$.

$x = \dfrac{\lambda D}{b} = \dfrac{(500\times10^{-9})(200\times10^{3})}{35\times10^{-2}} = 0.29\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses 200 m instead of 200 km for the orbital height.
perOption.B: Introduces an extra factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a lens diameter of 3.5 cm instead of 35 cm.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: The two lowest frequencies at which an open narrow tube resonates are 256 Hz and 512 Hz. If one of the ends is closed, what are the two lowest frequencies at which it would now resonate?
questions.stemText: The two lowest frequencies at which an open narrow tube resonates are 256 Hz and 512 Hz. If one of the ends is closed, what are the two lowest frequencies at which it would now resonate? A 128 Hz and 256 Hz B 128 Hz and 384 Hz C 384 Hz and 640 Hz D 768 Hz and 1536 Hz

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs to find the fundamental of the open tube and convert to the closed-tube harmonic series.
questions.misconception: Assuming closed tubes support all harmonics, or that closing an end raises frequency

explanation.body: The open tube has fundamental wavelength $2L$, so $v=f_0\lambda_0=(256)(2L)=512L$. With one end closed the longest resonant wavelength is $4L$, giving $f_1=512L/(4L)=128\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The next wavelength is $4L/3$, giving $f_2=512L/(4L/3)=384\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Includes the even harmonic at 256 Hz, which the tube with one closed end cannot support.
perOption.B: Correct. These are the fundamental and third harmonic.
perOption.C: Gives the third and fifth harmonics and skips the 128 Hz fundamental.
perOption.D: Both frequencies are even multiples of the new fundamental.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A narrow beam of monochromatic light falls at normal incidence on a diffraction grating. Third-order diffracted beams are formed at angles of $45^{\mathrm{o}}$ to the original direction.

What is the highest order of diffracted beam produced by this grating?
questions.stemText: A narrow beam of monochromatic light falls at normal incidence on a diffraction grating. Third-order diffracted beams are formed at angles of 45o to the original direction. What is the highest order of diffracted beam produced by this grating? A $3^{\mathrm{rd}}$ B $4^{\mathrm{th}}$ C $5^{\mathrm{th}}$ D $6^{\mathrm{th}}$

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding $d/\lambda$ from the given order and then the maximum integer with $\sin\theta \le 1$.
questions.misconception: Rounding up the maximum order or assuming 90° gives a visible order

explanation.body: For the third order, $d\sin45^\circ=3\lambda$. At the limiting angle of $90^\circ$, $d\sin90^\circ=n\lambda$. Combining these gives $n=4.24$ at the limit, so the highest allowed integer order is 4.

perOption.A: Stops at the observed order even though the fourth fits within the angular limit.
perOption.B: Correct. Four is the largest allowed integer order.
perOption.C: The fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.
perOption.D: The sixth order would also require $\sin\theta>1$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A wave pulse of length 0.25 m is shown at time t = 0. It moves along a string, fixed at point O, at 0.50 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. P is a point along the string 0.25 m from point O and 0.25 m from the pulse at t = 0.

Which graph best represents the displacement of point P with time for the period t = 1.5 s to t = 2.0 s?
questions.stemText: A wave pulse of length 0.25 m is shown at time t = 0. It moves along a string, fixed at point O, at 0.50 m s-1. P is a point along the string 0.25 m from point O and 0.25 m from the pulse at t = 0. 0.50 m s-1 P O 0.25 m 0.25 m 0.25 m Which graph best represents the displacement of point P with time for the period t = 1.5 s to t = 2.0 s? A displacement 0 t B displacement 0 t C displacement 0 t D displacement 0 t

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs timing of travel to and from the fixed end plus the phase inversion on reflection.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that a pulse reflected at a fixed end is inverted, or reversing the order of its parts

explanation.body: The pulse takes $0.25/0.50=0.5\ \mathrm s$ to travel $0.25\ \mathrm m$. Its leading edge reaches O at $1.0\ \mathrm s$, where the fixed end reflects and inverts the pulse. By $1.5\ \mathrm s$ that edge has travelled $0.75\ \mathrm m$ and reached P on its return. As the reflected pulse passes P between $1.5$ and $2.0\ \mathrm s$, P moves first through a larger upward displacement and then a smaller downward one.

perOption.A: Shows the smaller upward displacement first, reversing the order of the reflected lobes.
perOption.B: Shows the incoming pulse's displacement sequence, missing the inversion at the fixed end.
perOption.C: Inverts the lobes but puts the trailing lobe first.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm is directed perpendicular onto a diffraction grating. The third order diffraction lines are observed at $60^{\mathrm{o}}$ to each other.

What is the number of diffraction lines per millimetre of the grating?
questions.stemText: Monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm is directed perpendicular onto a diffraction grating. The third order diffraction lines are observed at 60o to each other. third order of diffraction third order of diffraction What is the number of diffraction lines per millimetre of the grating? A 333 B 507 C 667 D 333000

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs to halve the 60° angle before using d sinθ = nλ and to convert to lines per mm.
questions.misconception: Using the full angle between orders instead of the angle from the normal

explanation.body: The third-order maxima are symmetric, so each is at $\theta=60^\circ/2=30^\circ$ to the central direction. With line density $N=1/d$, the grating equation $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ gives $N=\sin30^\circ/(3\times500\times10^{-9})=3.33\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. This is $333$ lines per millimetre.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses an incorrect sine factor for the $30^\circ$ diffraction angle.
perOption.C: Drops the factor $\sin30^\circ=0.5$ from the line-density calculation.
perOption.D: Reports the line count per metre.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A Hubble telescope is used to observe two distant stars. The aperture diameter of the Hubble telescope is 2.4 m and visible light is used in the telescope. The two stars are observed to be just resolved.

Which is the best estimate for the angular separation of the two stars?
questions.stemText: A Hubble telescope is used to observe two distant stars. The aperture diameter of the Hubble telescope is 2.4 m and visible light is used in the telescope. The two stars are observed to be just resolved. Which is the best estimate for the angular separation of the two stars? A 1 x $10^{-8}$ rad B 2 x $10^{-7}$ rad C 1 x $10^{-5}$ rad D 2 x $10^{-5}$ rad

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the Rayleigh criterion with an estimated visible wavelength.
questions.misconception: Using a wrong wavelength order of magnitude for visible light

explanation.body: Using Rayleigh's criterion in the form $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, take $b=2.4\ \mathrm m$ and a typical visible wavelength $\lambda=500\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm m$. The stars are just resolved, so their separation is $\theta_{\min}\approx(500\times10^{-9})/2.4\approx2\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the diffraction limit by more than an order of magnitude.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the angular separation by about a factor of 50.
perOption.D: Overestimates the angular separation by about a factor of 100.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The diameter of the receiving dish of a telescope is 5.1 m. It receives light of wavelength $0.40\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ from two point sources at a distance of $2.8\times10^{25}\ \mathrm{m}$ away. What is the minimum separation of the two point sources so that the light from them can be resolved? A $1.1\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$ B $2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$ C $1.8\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{m}$ D $3.6\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{m}$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: The diameter of the receiving dish of a telescope is 5.1 m. It receives light of wavelength  25 0.40 μm from two point sources at a distance of away. 2.8 10 m

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1
DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of the Rayleigh criterion and small-angle geometry with large powers of ten.
questions.misconception: Inverting the ratio (dividing distance by angle) or using radius instead of diameter

explanation.body: Using the key's resolution approximation, $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the dish diameter. This gives $\theta_{\min}=(0.40\times10^{-6})/5.1=7.843\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{rad}$. For a small angle, the minimum separation is $x=\theta_{\min}D=(7.843\times10^{-8})(2.8\times10^{25})\approx2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Halves the separation, as would happen if the stated diameter were doubled.
perOption.B: Correct. This follows from the key's resolution approximation.
perOption.C: Inverts the angular ratio to $b/\lambda$ and halves the resulting separation.
perOption.D: Uses $b/\lambda$ instead of $\lambda/b$, giving a vastly larger separation.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A student blows gently across the top of a piece of glass tubing which is open at both ends. The fundamental frequency of sound produced is f.

While blowing, the student closes the lower end of the glass tubing.

What is the fundamental frequency of the sound produced?
questions.stemText: A student blows gently across the top of a piece of glass tubing which is open at both ends. The fundamental frequency of sound produced is f. While blowing, the student closes the lower end of the glass tubing. What is the fundamental frequency of the sound produced? A 4f B 2f C 0.5f D 0.25f

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard comparison of open–open and closed–open pipe fundamentals.
questions.misconception: Mixing up which pipe type has the longer fundamental wavelength

explanation.body: For the open tube’s fundamental, $\lambda/2=L$, so $f=v/(2L)$. With one end closed, the fundamental satisfies $\lambda_1/4=L$, so $f_1=v/(4L)=0.5f$.

perOption.A: Treats the quarter-wave condition as a fourfold frequency increase relative to the open tube.
perOption.B: Treats frequency as increasing when the fundamental wavelength doubles.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a quarter of the original frequency, overlooking that the open tube already contains only half a wavelength.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The human eye has an iris aperture of about 5 mm.

What is the minimum distance between two objects on a wall that are just resolved, if the wall is at 3.0 m from the eye?
questions.stemText: The human eye has an iris aperture of about 5 mm. What is the minimum distance between two objects on a wall that are just resolved, if the wall is at 3.0 m from the eye? A 0.0003 m B 0.003 m C 0.03 m D 0.3 m

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must estimate the wavelength of visible light and apply the Rayleigh criterion.
questions.misconception: Using the aperture size directly or a wrong order of magnitude for light's wavelength

explanation.body: Using the key’s Rayleigh estimate with visible light at about $500\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\sin\theta=\lambda/b=(500\times10^{-9})/(5\times10^{-3})$, so $\theta\approx0.0001\ \mathrm{rad}$. The minimum separation is approximately $3.0(0.0001)=0.0003\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of ten.
perOption.C: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of one hundred.
perOption.D: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of one thousand.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A camera lens with a maximum aperture of 25 mm forms an image of an object 9.0 m away.

If a monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm is used, what is the minimum distance between two points on the object that are just resolved?
questions.stemText: A camera lens with a maximum aperture of 25 mm forms an image of an object 9.0 m away. If a monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm is used, what is the minimum distance between two points on the object that are just resolved? A 0.090 mm B 0.18 mm C 5.2 mm D 10 mm

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct Rayleigh criterion with a small-angle conversion to separation.
questions.misconception: Applying the diffraction angle without multiplying by the object distance, or using radius instead of aperture width

explanation.body: Using the limiting angle $\theta \approx \lambda/b$, the minimum angular separation is $\frac{500\times10^{-9}}{25\times10^{-3}}=2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$. At $9.0\ \mathrm{m}$, the small-angle relation gives a minimum separation of $(9.0)(2.0\times10^{-5})=0.18\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Halves the calculated separation, which already represents the full gap between the points.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a separation much larger than the diffraction limit at the given distance.
perOption.D: Overestimates the limiting angle for a $25\ \mathrm{mm}$ aperture.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A sound wave resonates at its fundamental frequency $f$ in the following pipe of length $L$. [Diagram: pipe of length $L$ closed at one end, open at the other] In which of the following pipes would a sound wave of frequency $\tfrac{1}{2}f$ resonate in? [Options: pipes open at both ends] A length $L$ B length $2L$ C length $4L$ D length $6L$

stemImage.alt: Question 15: A sound wave resonates at its fundamental frequency f in the following pipe of length L. L 1 In which of the following pipes would a sound wave of frequency 2f

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Compare fundamental frequencies of closed and open pipes, then check harmonics.
questions.misconception: Treating open and closed pipes as having the same fundamental for the same length

explanation.body: The pipe closed at one end has fundamental wavelength $4L$, so the sound speed is $v=4fL$. At frequency $f/2$ the wavelength is $v/(f/2)=8L$. The fundamental of an open pipe fits half a wavelength, so its length is $4L$.

perOption.A: Uses an open pipe whose fundamental is $2f$, already above $f/2$.
perOption.B: Uses a quarter wavelength, which fits the fundamental of a pipe closed at one end.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Fits one and a half half-wavelengths, whereas an open pipe requires a whole number of half-wavelengths.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A beam of light that consists of all wavelengths between $480\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $600\ \mathrm{nm}$ is projected on a diffraction grating that contains 500 lines per millimetre. Excluding the central maximum, what is the maximum number of complete continuous spectra including overlapping spectra that can be observed emerging from the grating? A 3 B 6 C 7 D 8

stemImage.alt: Question 16: A beam of light that consists of all wavelengths between 480 nm and 600 nm is projected on a diffraction grating that contains 500 lines per millimetre. Excludi

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires using the longest wavelength to limit complete orders and counting both sides.
questions.misconception: Using the shortest wavelength, or forgetting orders on both sides

explanation.body: Use the longest wavelength, $600\ \mathrm{nm}$, because it diffracts through the largest angle in each order. With grating spacing $d=0.001/500\ \mathrm{m}$, $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ gives $\sin\theta=0.30n\leq1$. Orders 1 through 3 are complete on each side, giving six spectra.

perOption.A: Counts the complete spectra on only one side.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes the excluded central maximum.
perOption.D: Includes fourth orders, which lack the longest wavelengths.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Light waves from a single slit pass through a double-slit and interfere. The curved lines represent wavefronts. At which point does complete destructive interference occur? [Diagram: a single slit on the left produces curved wavefronts reaching a double slit; two sets of curved wavefronts spread from the double slit and overlap. A labels a point at the upper slit edge; B is a point on the central axis where crests from both slits meet; C labels a point on one crest midway between two crests of the other set; D labels the centre of a diamond between intersecting crests.]

stemImage.alt: Question 15: Light waves from a single slit pass through a double-slit and interfere. The curved lines represent wavefronts. At which point does complete destructive interfe

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard crest/trough reading of a two-source wavefront diagram.
questions.misconception: Thinking the gap between wavefronts (trough-trough) gives cancellation

explanation.body: Complete destructive interference occurs where a crest from one slit meets a trough from the other. At C, a curved wavefront from one slit is halfway between successive wavefronts from the other slit.

perOption.A: A is at the upper slit, before the two outgoing waves overlap there.
perOption.B: B lies on the central line, where both waves travel equal distances and arrive in phase.
perOption.C: Correct. A crest meets a trough.
perOption.D: D is where two drawn wavefronts meet, so the waves arrive in phase.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An optical telescope received yellow light of wavelength $6\times10^{-7}$ m from two yellow stars which are $1\times10^{11}$ m apart and can just be resolved by the telescope. The two stars are $6\times10^{16}$ m from the telescope. Which statement is incorrect? A The aperture of the telescope has a diameter of about 0.4 m. B The resolving power of the telescope depends on both the wavelength of light received and the aperture diameter of the telescope. C The telescope receiving red light of wavelength $7\times10^{-7}$ m can be used to resolve two red stars of the same separation and distance from the telescope as the two yellow stars. D The telescope receiving yellow light of wavelength $6\times10^{-7}$ m can be used to resolve another pair of yellow stars that are separated by $3\times10^{-6}$ radians.

stemImage.alt: Question 16: An optical telescope received yellow light of wavelength 6  10–7 m from two yellow stars which are 1  1011 m apart and can just be resolved by the telescope.

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs computing angular separation and aperture from Rayleigh criterion, then checking each statement.
questions.misconception: Thinking a longer wavelength improves resolution

explanation.body: Using $s=r\theta$, the yellow stars subtend $\theta=1.7\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$. With $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, the aperture diameter is $b\approx0.35\ \mathrm{m}$, or about $0.4\ \mathrm{m}$. Red light has a longer wavelength, so its minimum resolvable angle exceeds the unchanged angular separation of the stars.

perOption.A: The yellow-light limit gives an aperture diameter of about $0.4\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.B: The resolution criterion depends on both $\lambda$ and the aperture diameter.
perOption.C: Correct. The red stars are too close in angle to resolve.
perOption.D: The new separation of $3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$ exceeds the yellow-light resolution limit.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Monochromatic light of wavelength 520 nm is directed perpendicularly onto a diffraction grating. The second-order diffraction lines are observed at $56°$ to each other.

[Diagram: light of wavelength 520 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating; the two second-order beams diverge to a screen with an angle of $56°$ between them.]

What is the total number of diffraction lines produced by the grating?

A 4   B 5   C 8   D 9

stemImage.alt: Question 15: Monochromatic light of wavelength 520 nm is directed perpendicularly onto a diffraction grating. The second-order diffraction lines are observed at 56 to each

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must halve the angle, find $d/\lambda$ and then count the orders on both sides plus the central maximum.
questions.misconception: Using 56° rather than 28° as the diffraction angle, or forgetting the central maximum

explanation.body:
The second-order lines are $56°$ apart, so each is at $\theta = 28°$: $d\sin 28° = 2\lambda \Rightarrow \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°}$.

From $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ and $\sin\theta \le 1$: $n \le \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°} = 4.26$, so $n_{\max} = 4$.

Number of diffraction lines $= (4 \times 2) + 1 = 9$

perOption.A: Gives only the highest order, $n_{\max}$, instead of counting lines on both sides and the central maximum.
perOption.B: Counts only one side of the central maximum, plus the zeroth order.
perOption.C: Counts both sides but leaves out the zeroth-order (central) line.
perOption.D: Correct. $n_{\max} = 4$ on each side, plus the central maximum.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two stars are at a distance of 20 light years from the Earth. An optical telescope with an aperture of 3.0 m is used to view the stars.

A light year is the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year which is approximately $10^{16}$ m.

What is the order of magnitude of the minimum separation between the two stars that can just be resolved by the telescope?
questions.stemText: Two stars are at a distance of 20 light years from the Earth. An optical telescope with an aperture of 3.0 m is used to view the stars. A light year is the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year which is approximately 1016 m. What is the order of magnitude of the minimum separation between the two stars that can just be resolved by the telescope? A $10^{8}$ m B $10^{10}$ m C $10^{12}$ m D $10^{14}$ m

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must choose a visible wavelength themselves and combine the Rayleigh criterion with the small-angle approximation.

explanation.body:
Distance $r = 20 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}$. By the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta \approx \lambda/D$, so the minimum separation is $s = r\theta = r\dfrac{\lambda}{D}$.

Violet (400 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(400 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 2.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Red (700 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(700 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 4.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Across the visible range, the order of magnitude is $10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too small by a factor of about 100, likely from a powers-of-ten slip in $r$ or $\lambda$.
perOption.B: Correct. $s = r\lambda/D \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$ for visible light.
perOption.C: Too large by a factor of about 100, likely from a powers-of-ten slip in $\lambda$ (for example, using micrometres as nanometres).
perOption.D: Far too large. It does not follow from $s = r\lambda/D$ with visible wavelengths.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which statement concerning a stationary wave is correct?
questions.stemText: Which statement concerning a stationary wave is correct? A All the particles between two successive nodes oscillate in phase. B There is no displacement of a particle at an antinode at any time. C The wavelength of the stationary wave is equal to the separation of two adjacent nodes. D The amplitude of the stationary wave is equal to the amplitude of one of the waves creating it.

options.label: A
options.text: All the particles between two successive nodes oscillate in phase.

options.label: B
options.text: There is no displacement of a particle at an antinode at any time.

options.label: C
options.text: The wavelength of the stationary wave is equal to the separation of two adjacent nodes.

options.label: D
options.text: The amplitude of the stationary wave is equal to the amplitude of one of the waves creating it.

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Identify the standard phase, spacing and amplitude properties of a stationary wave.
questions.misconception: Confusing nodes with antinodes

explanation.body: Particles between successive nodes oscillate in phase. A node has zero displacement at all times, and adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength. At an antinode, the amplitude is twice that of either component wave.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A node is the point with zero displacement at all times.
perOption.C: Adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength.
perOption.D: At an antinode, the amplitude is twice that of either component wave.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Progressive sound waves of wavelength 20 cm enter four pipes.

In which pipes are standing waves formed?
questions.stemText: Progressive sound waves of wavelength 20 cm enter four pipes. pipe type length / cm P closed at one end 25 Q closed at one end 30 R open at both ends 30 S open at both ends 35 In which pipes are standing waves formed? A P and R only B P and S only C Q and R only D Q and S only

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Apply different resonance conditions to open and closed pipes.
questions.misconception: Applying the same resonance condition to both pipe types

explanation.body: A pipe open at both ends supports standing waves when $L=n\lambda/2$ for a positive integer $n$. With $\lambda=20\ \mathrm{cm}$, pipe R fits three half wavelengths. A pipe closed at one end requires $L=(2n-1)\lambda/4$, so pipe P fits five quarter wavelengths.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Pipe S cannot fit a whole number of half wavelengths between its open ends.
perOption.C: Pipe Q fits six quarter wavelengths, but a pipe closed at one end needs an odd number.
perOption.D: Pipe Q fails the odd-quarter-wavelength condition and pipe S fails the whole-half-wavelength condition.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Graph 1 shows a transverse wave moving to its right.

Graph 2 shows a standing wave on a string stretched between two points X and Y.

Positions of particles P, Q, R, S, T, A, B, C, D and E are indicated in the two figures.

[Graph 1 shows successive crests P and Q, with trough S between them. R and T are on opposite sides of S at the same displacement below the equilibrium line. An arrow labelled $v$ points right. Graph 2 shows three loops between X and Y. A and E are the peaks of the outer loops, C is the trough of the middle loop, and B and D are on opposite sides of C within that loop.]

Which of the following statements regarding the particles is not correct?

A. Graph 1: P and S are in antiphase. Graph 2: A and C are in antiphase.
B. Graph 1: P and Q are in phase. Graph 2: A and E are in phase.
C. Graph 1: Q and S are in antiphase. Graph 2: B and E are in antiphase.
D. Graph 1: R and T are out of phase. Graph 2: B and D are out of phase.

stemImage.alt: Question 14: Graph 1 shows a transverse wave moving to its right. Graph 2 shows a standing wave on a string stretched between two points X and Y. Positions of particles P, Q

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires comparing phase in a progressive wave with phase within and between standing-wave loops.
questions.misconception: Applying progressive-wave phase rules within a standing-wave loop

explanation.body: In the standing wave, B and D are in the same loop, so they oscillate in phase. This makes the Graph 2 statement in option D incorrect. The other seven statements are correct.

perOption.A: Both statements are true because P and S are half a wavelength apart and A and C are in adjacent loops.
perOption.B: Both statements are true because P and Q are one wavelength apart and A and E are separated by two loops.
perOption.C: Both statements are true because Q and S are half a wavelength apart and B and E are in adjacent loops.
perOption.D: Correct. B and D oscillate in phase.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $490\ \mathrm{nm}$ falls normally on a diffraction grating that has $6\times10^5$ lines per metre. Which one of the following is correct?

A The first order is observed at angle of diffraction of $12^\circ$.
B The third and higher orders are not produced.
C A grating with more lines per metre could produce more orders.
D Total number of maximas produced is 7.

stemImage.alt: Question 19: Monochromatic light of wavelength 490 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating that has 6 x 105 lines per metre. Which one of the following is correct?

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert line density to spacing, bound the order and count both sides.
questions.misconception: The highest order equals the number of maxima.

explanation.body: Use $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, with $d=1/(6\times10^5)\ \mathrm{m}$. For $n=1$, $\sin\theta=(490\times10^{-9})/d$ gives $\theta=17^\circ$. Since $\sin\theta\leq1$, $n\leq d/\lambda=3.4$, so the highest order is 3. There are $2(3)+1=7$ maxima including the central maximum.

perOption.A: The grating equation gives a first-order angle of $17^\circ$.
perOption.B: The third order is still allowed because $3\lambda/d<1$.
perOption.C: Increasing the line density decreases the spacing and lowers the upper bound on the order.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The slit separation of the diffraction grating is $2.8\lambda$. How many diffraction maxima are present in the transmitted light?
A 2
B 4
C 5
D 7

stemImage.alt: Question 13: Monochromatic light of wavelength  is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The slit separation of the diffraction grating is 2.8. How many diffraction

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires finding the greatest allowed integer order and counting maxima on both sides of the centre.
questions.misconception: Omitting the central maximum

explanation.body: The grating equation is $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$. At $\theta=90^\circ$, the upper bound on $n$ is $2.8\lambda\sin90^\circ/\lambda=2.8$, so the highest integer order is 2. There are $2\times2+1=5$ maxima including the central maximum.

perOption.A: Counts only the first and second orders on one side.
perOption.B: Counts both pairs of side maxima but omits the central maximum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the upper bound up and includes an impossible third order on each side.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A stationary sound wave is formed in a pipe of length $L$ that is closed at one end. The stationary sound wave has two nodes. What is the wavelength of the stationary wave?
A $L/4$
B $3L/4$
C $4L/3$
D $4L/5$

stemImage.alt: Question 14: A stationary sound wave is formed in a pipe of length L that is closed at one end. The stationary sound wave has two nodes. What is the wavelength of the statio

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The end conditions and node count determine how many quarter wavelengths fit in the pipe.
questions.misconception: Miscounting quarter wavelengths between the end conditions

explanation.body: The two-node pattern has a displacement node at the closed end, one interior node, and an antinode at the open end. The pipe length contains three quarters of a wave, so $L=3\lambda/4$ and $\lambda=4L/3$.

perOption.A: Mistakes the quarter-wave segment length for the wavelength.
perOption.B: Applies the factor $3/4$ to $L$ when solving $L=3\lambda/4$ for $\lambda$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Fits five quarter wavelengths, producing three displacement nodes.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A compact spectrometer uses a diffraction grating containing $4.0\times10^5$ lines per metre. White light with wavelengths from $420\ \mathrm{nm}$ to $680\ \mathrm{nm}$ is incident normally on the grating.

[White light travels horizontally to a vertical grating. Beyond it a ray continues horizontally, and the first-order red and blue rays angle upwards, with red above blue. The angle between the red and blue rays is $\theta$.]

What is the angular separation between the blue and red ends of the first-order spectrum?

A $6.1^\circ$
B $9.7^\circ$
C $15.8^\circ$
D $25.5^\circ$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: 4 0 10 lines per metre. White 5 A compact spectrometer uses a diffraction grating containing .  light with wavelengths from 420 nm to 680 nm is incident normal

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Find the grating spacing, then calculate and subtract two diffraction angles.
questions.misconception: Confusing an angle from the grating normal with the angular separation.

explanation.body:
Use $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ with $n=1$ and $d=1/(4.0\times10^5)\ \mathrm{m}$. The blue end at $420\ \mathrm{nm}$ is at $9.67^\circ$ and the red end at $680\ \mathrm{nm}$ is at $15.8^\circ$.

Their separation is $15.8^\circ-9.67^\circ=6.13^\circ$, or $6.1^\circ$ to the precision of the options.

perOption.A: Correct. It is the difference between the two first-order angles.
perOption.B: Uses only the angle of the blue ray from the normal.
perOption.C: Uses only the angle of the red ray from the normal.
perOption.D: Adds the angles as if the rays were on opposite sides of the normal.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A parallel beam of monochromatic light passes through a narrow slit and forms a diffraction pattern on a distant screen. The width x is the distance between the first minima on either side
questions.stemText: A parallel beam of monochromatic light passes through a narrow slit and forms a diffraction pattern on a distant screen. The width x is the distance between the first minima on either side of the central maximum. Which statement is incorrect? A Moving the screen closer to the slit increases x. B Increasing the slit width generally allows more light to pass through the slit. C Increasing the slit width decreases x. D Increasing the wavelength increases x.

options.label: A
options.text: Moving the screen closer to the slit increases x.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing the slit width generally allows more light to pass through the slit.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the slit width decreases x.

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Relate the angular position of the first minimum to the width measured on the screen.
questions.misconception: Confusing angular width with width on the screen.

explanation.body: The first minimum satisfies $b\sin\theta=\lambda$, so $\theta\approx\lambda/b$ for small angles. At screen distance $D$, the central maximum has width $x\approx 2D\theta\approx 2D\lambda/b$. Bringing the screen closer decreases $D$ and therefore decreases $x$, so A is the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: Correct. Bringing the screen closer decreases $x$.
perOption.B: This statement is true because a wider slit lets more light through.
perOption.C: This statement is true because increasing $b$ reduces $x$.
perOption.D: This statement is true because increasing $\lambda$ increases $x$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Two coherent wave sources, $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$, emit light waves of the same frequency but different intensity. The intensity of the wave from $S_{1}$ is 4I while the intensity of the wave from $S_{2}$ is I. The waves meet at point P to form a bright fringe due to constructive interference and meet at point Q to form a dark fringe due to destructive interference. What is the ratio of the intensity of light at point P to the intensity of light at point Q?
questions.stemText: Two coherent wave sources, S1 and S2, emit light waves of the same frequency but different intensity. The intensity of the wave from S1 is 4I while the intensity of the wave from S2 is I. The waves meet at point P to form a bright fringe due to constructive interference and meet at point Q to form a dark fringe due to destructive interference. What is the ratio of the intensity of light at point P to the intensity of light at point Q? A 0.11 B 1.7 C 4.0 D 9.0

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting intensities to amplitudes before combining and squaring them.
questions.misconception: Adding or subtracting intensities directly.

explanation.body: Since $I=kA^2$, if the amplitude from $S_2$ is $A$, the amplitude from $S_1$ is $2A$. The resultant amplitude is $2A+A=3A$ at P and $2A-A=A$ at Q. Thus $\frac{I_P}{I_Q}=\frac{(3A)^2}{A^2}=9.0$.

perOption.A: Reverses the bright-to-dark intensity ratio.
perOption.B: Adds and subtracts intensities directly, giving $5/3$.
perOption.C: Uses the source intensity ratio without combining the waves.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Light of wavelength 690 nm passes through a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm, producing a series of bright spots (maxima) on a screen.

What is the total number of bright spots that are produced?
questions.stemText: Light of wavelength 690 nm passes through a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm, producing a series of bright spots (maxima) on a screen. What is the total number of bright spots that are produced? A 4 B 8 C 9 D 11

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting line density to spacing, finding the highest integer order and counting both sides.
questions.misconception: Omitting the zero-order maximum.

explanation.body: Use $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$. At $\theta=90^\circ$, $\frac{1}{300\times1000}\sin90^\circ=n(690\times10^{-9})$, giving an order limit of about $4.83$. The highest observable integer order is $4$, so there are $4+1+4=9$ bright spots.

perOption.A: Counts the nonzero orders on only one side.
perOption.B: Omits the central maximum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the order limit up to five even though the fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.
